Multiple-decrement CoDa model of causes of death (experimental)

Source: R/model-coda.R
coda_causes.Rd

coda_causes() forecasts death rates by cause with the multiple-decrement form of the compositional Lee-Carter model, which Oeppen (2008) proposed and tested on Japanese causes of death. Causes add up to all causes in every draw. The model is experimental. Status: published, with the deviations listed below; section numbers refer to Oeppen (2008).

Usage

coda_causes(
  var = "cause",
  total_level = "all",
  jump_off = c("observed", "fitted"),
  residual = "auto",
  rank = 1,
  order = c(0, 1, 1),
  drift = TRUE
)

Arguments

var

Stratum variable with the causes.

total_level

Level of var for all causes.

jump_off

"observed" (forecasts start from the observed deaths of the last year) or "fitted" (from the fitted deaths).

residual

Add a residual cause, the part of all-cause mortality not covered by the listed causes: TRUE, FALSE, or "auto" (added when the listed causes leave more than 0.1% of all-cause mortality unexplained in the median cell).

rank

Number of components (1 by default; Oeppen 2008 used 2 for Japan).

order, drift

ARIMA order and drift of each index, as in coda().

Value

A model specification.

Details

Model (Sections 3, 6 and 8.3). In each group (the strata that differ only in var, for example one group per sex):

  1. the cause-specific rates m[x, c] add up to all-cause rates m[x], which give life-table deaths d[x] with radix 1 (life_table() conventions); the deaths are split by cause, d[x, c] = d[x] m[x, c] / m[x] (relations of the multiple-decrement life table, eq. 1 and 7);

  2. the array of deaths by age and cause of each year is unfolded into one composition (Section 6), plus the survivors at the upper bound of a closed age range;

  3. the compositions are centred by their closed geometric mean over the years and transformed by the centred log-ratio; the first rank components of a singular value decomposition give sum_j b_j[x, c] k_j[t] (Section 3, steps 1-7);

  4. forecast deaths d[x, c] give all-cause rates from the all-cause life-table deaths d[x] = sum_c d[x, c], and cause-specific rates m[x, c] = m[x] d[x, c] / d[x] (eq. 7, Section 8.3).

The causes add up to the all-cause rates in every draw, and the strata of total_level get their sum. If the listed causes leave part of the all-cause deaths unexplained (residual), that part is a residual cause inside the model and counts towards the all-cause rates; it is not a stratum of the output (package-specific).

Indexes and rank. For Japanese women 1951-1990, Oeppen (2008, Sections 6 and 7) uses two components and selects ARIMA(0,2,2) models for the indexes by AICc; Section 3 notes, for the Lee-Carter model, that one component is usually adequate for advanced economies and that its index can be forecast by a simple ARIMA model such as the random walk with drift. These choices belong to one data set; the defaults here are one component and the index model of coda(), ARIMA(0,1,1) with drift (Bergeron-Boucher et al. 2017, with Oeppen as co-author). rank = 2, order = c(0, 2, 2) gives Oeppen's specification for Japan. With several components, each index has its own ARIMA model, independent of the others (the paper does not say how the second index was forecast).

Deviations from the paper. Oeppen (2008) gives point forecasts only: the jump-off (forecasts start from the observed deaths of the last year, jump_off = "observed") and the draws (bootstrap of the residuals and of the index paths, centred on the point forecast) are those of coda() (Bergeron-Boucher et al. 2017, Appendices B and G). Oeppen (2008, Section 3) replaces zero counts by lightly smoothing the deaths of each year with a penalised histogram smoother whose smoothing parameter is not given; here zero counts are replaced multiplicatively in the composition of each year (Bergeron-Boucher et al. 2017, Appendix C; see coda()). How the death rate of the open age interval follows from the forecast deaths is not stated; here the all-cause log rate of an open interval is regressed on the indexes and split by cause through the composition (package-specific, as open = "regression" of coda()).

Draws are expected rates. Predictive draws (mt_forecast(predictive = TRUE)) draw Poisson all-cause deaths given the all-cause rates and exposures and split them multinomially between the causes by the cause shares of the draw, so that the causes also add up to all causes in predictive draws; no other observation noise is added (package-specific).

The extensions of Kjærgaard, Ergemen, Kallestrup-Lamb, Oeppen and Lindahl-Jacobsen (2019) are not implemented, nor is the alpha-transformation that Dong, Shang, Hui and Bruhn (2025) use in place of the clr for compositions of causes with zero counts. Compare the model with reconciled() separate models in a backtest before using it.

References

Oeppen J (2008). Coherent forecasting of multiple-decrement life tables: a test using Japanese cause of death data. CODAWORK'08, Universitat de Girona. https://hdl.handle.net/10256/742

Bergeron-Boucher M-P, Canudas-Romo V, Oeppen J, Vaupel JW (2017). Coherent forecasts of mortality with compositional data analysis. Demographic Research 37(17): 527-566. doi:10.4054/DemRes.2017.37.17

Kjærgaard S, Ergemen YE, Kallestrup-Lamb M, Oeppen J, Lindahl-Jacobsen R (2019). Forecasting causes of death by using compositional data analysis: the case of cancer deaths. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series C 68(5): 1351-1370. doi:10.1111/rssc.12357

Dong Z, Shang HL, Hui F, Bruhn A (2025). A compositional approach to modeling cause-specific mortality with zero counts. Annals of Actuarial Science 19(3): 416-441. doi:10.1017/S1748499524000320

See also

reconciled() with a hierarchy of causes, coda().

Examples

x <- mt_example_causes(years = 2005:2019)
fit <- mt_fit(coda_causes(), x)
fc <- mt_forecast(fit, h = 5, n_draws = 50, seed = 1)
